article.title: Expand or Contract? On Member Voting Rights
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Vincent Lima In our September General Meeting, members of ROC DSA wisely rejected a proposal that would restrict their right to vote on certain key decisions. The rejected proposal appeared to be part of a broader movement to shrink the voting base of DSA. Our process for considering applications for the endorsement of candidates for elected office has been tweaked from time to time, but the main steps have remained: The candidate submits an application signed by a certain number of ROC DSA members. The application includes a questionnaire. The signature requirement signifies some baseline level of support and at least hints at the candidate’s ability to collect signatures on a petition. In reality, the chapter does not passively await applications, but the application is what formally kicks off the process. The Electoral Working Group vets the applicant. The group is open to all members. Thus, all members can engage on this level, but no member is required to do so. The EWG makes a recommendation regarding endorsement and forwards the package to the Steering Committee. A candidate forum is scheduled. Every member is welcome to listen to and interact with the candidate. This process should include deliberation. In other words, members should be able to discuss their thoughts about the candidacy in light of the forum and in light of the chapter’s broader strategic goals. The Steering Committee, which is the chapter’s elected political leadership, makes a recommendation. A ballot is sent to all members to vote Yes or No on the endorsement. Crucially, the ballot includes links to the candidate’s application, the minutes of the candidate forum, and the recommendations of the EWG and Steering Committee. The step that has been made contentious is the last. The proposal was to restrict voting on the endorsement to members who attended the deliberative meeting. This proposal to restrict the vote is made in the name of democracy. I will turn to Marx for a moment—not because he is necessary for this argument but because some advocates for limiting the franchise claim to be Marxists and argue that a universal franchise is a mockery of democracy; it is merely “bourgeois democracy.” Marx appreciated “bourgeois democracy” for extending the franchise (the right to vote) but noted accurately that not everyone has the time and inclination to engage in the democratic process. “Universal Suffrage is the equivalent for political power for the working class,” Marx wrote in the New-York Daily Tribute in 1852. In Capital, vol. 1 (1867; trans. Paul Reitter, 2024), he added (p. 235), A worker self-evidently lives [their] whole life as nothing but labor-power. Thus, by nature and by right, all [their] disposable time is labor-time that belongs to capital’s process of self-valorization. Time spent on human and intellectual growth or social functions and interactions or the free play of vital physical and mental powers, or even time spent resting on Sundays—it’s all just a waste! Lenin, in State and Revolution (1917), elaborated: “Owing to the conditions of capitalist exploitation, the modern wage slaves are so crushed by want and poverty that they ‘cannot be bothered with democracy,’ and ‘cannot be bothered with politics’; in the ordinary, peaceful course of events, the majority of the population is debarred from participation in public and political life.” Thanks to organized labor and popular movements, many of us have more time for “public and political life” than the workers described above. Still, to say, “If you can’t make the meeting, you can’t vote,” is not to take a Marxist position. The counterargument is that democracy is not just about voting; it is more about process than outcome. Indeed, it is crucially important to provide every opportunity for members to participate in the process. But voting is not a reward for participation; it is an element of participation. How do we make it possible for comrades who have to engage in social production and reproduction to participate in the democratic process? Or, in normal-people language, if you have to make a living and take care of yourself or your dependents—by going to school, caring for a child, looking after an elder, going on vacation, or whatever you will—do we tell you, “Too bad; you are canceled”? How do we include everyone? Our hybrid meetings are a great step. You can’t attend in person? Attend remotely and save the time and expense it would take to commute, or participate while keeping an eye on the baby. Our Slack debates are not great; they often consist of walls of text dominated mostly by a handful of men with time on their hands. But Slack is still an available venue for debate. Offline conversations, too, are part of member engagement. Say I pick up the phone and contact a fellow member to say, “Mary is running and I think we should back her. What do you think? OK. Don’t forget to vote when the ballot comes!” That is exactly what we should be doing to involve people in our campaigns! Showing up to meetings is but one form of involvement. I do it. Maybe you do it. But it’s not for everyone. Some members may not have the time, as discussed above. Others may just not want to do it. Maybe listening to another speech “in favor” is more than they can bear. Maybe Robert’s Rules get under their skin and all they want to do is knock on doors and talk to their neighbors about socialism. I embrace them and welcome them and insist that they have a vote.
